title: Others before themselves
hookLine: the Ansar preferred others over themselves even in need (59:9)

lines: ONE MEAL, JUST FOR THE CHILDREN.
cards: A guest knocks at night. The family has one small meal in the house, just enough for the children. The husband and wife look at each other.

They put the children to bed hungry, set the food before the guest, and the wife gets up, as if to fix the lamp, and puts it out. In the dark, the couple move their hands and mouths as if they're eating.
The guest eats his fill. Nobody sees that nobody else ate. Except, the hadith says, someone did.

teach.h: A GUEST, A LAMP PUT OUT.
teach.b: Bukhari and Muslim tell the story. A hungry man came to the Prophet ﷺ, who had nothing at home, and asked who would host him.
A man of the Ansar, the Helpers of Medina, took him home; Muslim's report names him Abu Talha. In the morning, the Prophet told him God had marveled at what he and his wife had done for their guest.

And the reports say this verse came down. Pickthall: they "prefer (the fugitives) above themselves though poverty become their lot." The fugitives are the Muhajirun, the emigrants who had fled Mecca with almost nothing.
The Ansar had taken them in, shared homes, fields, even work.
The verse praises them for three things: they love those who came to them, they feel no envy for what the newcomers were given, and they prefer them over themselves.
That last is ithar, from the root '-th-r, to choose, to give preference. It's more than generosity. Generosity gives from extra.
Ithar gives when there's no extra, when you'd go without.

teach.h: SAVED FROM THE GREED OF THE SOUL.
teach.b: The verse ends: whoever is saved from the greed of his own soul, those are the successful. So the hardest part isn't the giving. It's the inner grip, the voice that says, but I need it too.
Some writers on character call ithar the highest rank of generosity. The hadith gives it a picture: a darkened room, and a lamp put out on purpose, so a guest would think his hosts were eating too.

how: Muslims tell the story of the Ansari couple and their guest as the model of ithar, and hospitality to guests, even when little is at hand, is a strongly emphasized virtue in Muslim communities.

o: preferring others over yourself, even in need
giving charity from what you have left over
hosting guests only when you have plenty

games.q: ithar in Al-Hashr — tap the pairs.
p: put out so the guest would eat

s: ithar means giving only from what you have extra
it means preferring others even when you're in need yourself.
the Ansari couple put out the lamp so the guest wouldn't notice they weren't eating
Bukhari and Muslim tell the story.
the verse praises the Ansar for feeling no envy for what the emigrants were given
they love those who came to them and feel no need in their hearts for what was given.

games.q: you're the Ansari wife. there's one small meal, for the children, and a guest at the table. what do you do?
o: serve the children and apologize to the guest.
put the children to sleep, serve the guest, and put out the lamp.
split the meal into tiny portions.
games.why: she put out the lamp so the couple could pretend to eat. the Prophet said God had marveled at what they did.

practice: Think through your day, a parking spot, the last slice, the first turn to talk, credit for something done together, and find one place you could quietly let someone else have it.
Notice the small grip inside that says, but I want it, and breathe into it.

wordCard.voice: Ithar. Preferring others over yourself, even when you're in need, as the Ansar did for the emigrants. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: ithar, preferring others over oneself. From the root '-th-r; the verse uses yu'thiruna, they prefer.

carryVoice: Your line: others first. A lamp went out so a guest could eat. Day six hundred eighteen, done.
